newsitem.title: UK: Pound shrugs off opinion polls, firms against mark.
newsitem.headline: Pound shrugs off opinion polls, firms against mark.

text.p: The pound shrugged off a new opinion poll showing a sharp fall in the opposition Labour party's lead just over a week before polling day, choosing instead to track the firm dollar, traders said.
An ICM poll in the Guardian newspaper showed Labour's lead slumped from 14 to five points, the first time the opposition's lead has fallen to single digits since November 1993.
But worries in the market about Labour's shrinking lead were offset by a rolling Gallup poll in today's Daily Telegraph which put Labour 21 points ahead, an inrease of five in a week.

"The conflicting polls left the market a bit unsure what to do, but after some initial pound selling it has rallied again, supported by the firm tone of the dollar," said David Coleman, chief economist at CIBC Wood Gundy.
At 0932 GMT the pound traded at 2.8020/30 marks, up about a pfennig from morning lows but still down a touch from Tuesday's European close at 2.8050/60.
Against the dollar, the pound was slightly easier at $1.6340/50 from $1.6365/75.

Coleman said the market would only be concerned if opinion polls continued to show a decline in Labour's lead. "I don't think there will be much concern unless all the remaining polls suggest Labour's lead is shrinking dramatically," he said.

The conflicting polls also stirred up memories of how wrong the pollsters got it in the 1992 election, traders said. The five major polling organisations forecast a Labour lead, but the Conservatives swept back into power. UK financial markets, having priced in a Labour victory in the May 1 election, would be susceptible to selling if the poll results in a hung parliament, analysts said.
A Labour victory is unlikely to shake the pound because the party's economic policies are not fundamentally different from those of the current Conservative government, analysts said.

Despite Labour's transformation, its image is still tarred with the high spending, high taxation and high inflation reputation it gained in the late 1970s. "Even though investors are pretty sanguine about a Labour government, another Conservative administration would still be favoured," said Paul Meggyesi, senior currency economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell.
Some traders might consider positioning for a repeat of the 1992 post-election bounce in UK financial markets after the Conservatives grabbed a surprise last minute victory, Meggyesi added.
British retail sales data for March were seen as neutral for the pound. Retail sales rose 0.3 percent from the previous month, in line with market forecasts.

The minutes of the March monetary meeting, released this morning, showed that Bank of England Governor Eddie George again called fro a quarter point rise in interest rates. But Chancellor Kenneth Clarke decided to leave rates on hold.
